definition: The program whose whole job is listening to your keyboard in a terminal. It reads each line, decides what you meant, and runs it — a translator between you and your computer, not magic.
The window where you type commands. Once a physical device, now an app that pretends to be one — the shell lives inside it.
The physical global network — undersea cables, routers, data centres — that carries data between computers. The road. The web is just one vehicle that uses it.
Short for World Wide Web — the system of hyperlinked pages, URLs, and HTTP that runs on top of the internet. Invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989, given away for free.
A small chunk of data — a few hundred to about 1,500 bytes — sent independently with an address header and reassembled on arrival. Nothing on the internet travels as one piece.
A unique number identifying a device on the network, like a house address for packets. Your public IP changes; private IPs live inside your home network.
The original addressing system — four numbers from 0 to 255, separated by dots. About 4.3 billion addresses; the pool ran dry in 2011.
The modern addressing system — long hexadecimal addresses with room for so many devices that every grain of sand on Earth could have one.
The protocol that guarantees delivery: confirms the connection, acknowledges every packet, re-sends lost ones, and reorders arrivals. IP's responsible older sibling.
A fast protocol that makes zero promises — no handshake, no re-sending. Used where speed beats perfection: video calls, games, live streams.
The device that directs packets between networks — the traffic cop of the internet. In your home, it also translates public and private IP addresses (NAT).
Network Address Translation — the trick that lets one public IP address serve every device on your home network by translating between outside and inside addresses.
The 1969 US defense research network built to survive a nuclear attack — the internet's ancestor, and the reason the internet has no centre.
Whatever initiates a request. A browser, an app, curl, a Python script — even another server. Not a type of machine; a role in the conversation.
Whatever listens for requests and answers them. Not a special machine — any computer told to sit and wait. Your laptop becomes one when you run a dev server.
The web's fundamental relationship: one side always asks (client), one side always answers (server). Asymmetric by design — the server never initiates.
The client's half of the conversation: 'may I have this thing?' A message asking a server for data or an action.
The server's half of the conversation: the answer to a request — the data asked for, or an explanation of why it couldn't be done.
'This computer, right here.' A loopback address where client and server are the same machine — the whole market stall happening inside your laptop during development.
A network model with no fixed server — every machine is both client and server, talking directly. BitTorrent and blockchain work this way. The web does not.
A client that does almost no work itself — it just displays what the server sends. The early web's browser: fully-rendered HTML arrives, the browser shows it.
A client that does the heavy lifting itself — the server sends data, the client assembles the interface. Modern SPAs like Gmail and Twitter.
